newsitem.title: JAPAN: BOJ shifting policy focus slightly toward prices.
newsitem.headline: BOJ shifting policy focus slightly toward prices.

text.p: The Bank of Japan (BOJ) has shifted some of its focus to watching inflation amid rising import prices, but its monetary policy will still be aimed at strengthening the economic recovery, BOJ officials said on Friday.

BOJ governor Yasuo Matsushita told a news conference on Friday that the central bank needed to watch prices carefully as recent import prices had risen sharply and the likelihood of a sustainable recovery was becoming stronger.
Senior BOJ officials acknowledged that there has been a slight change in the BOJ's view of the economy due to the rise in import prices.

"It's true that there has been a slight change of 'nuance' in the way we look at the economy, although it will not change the priority of our policy -- that is to strengthen the basis of the recovery," one senior official told Reuters.
"The feeling is that now we do have one eye on prices," he added.
Japan's import prices for the first 20 days of February showed a hefty rise of 16.5 percent from February of the previous year, according to data released by the BOJ.
"The tempo of the rise in import prices has accelerated recently, on the back of the recent weakening of the yen and a rise in crude oil prices," Matsushita said.
The yen has weakened around 15 percent from a year ago, standing at around 120.40 to the dollar in late Tokyo on Friday from around 104.80 at the end of February 1996.
"We don't expect inflation to appear any time soon, but if there were to be a change in interest rates, it would be backed up by a recovery in the economy," the senior official said.
He said that unless the yen were to weaken further, any clear rise in prices would be alongside a stronger economy, so that growth would be able to stand up to a credit tightening.

Although the official said it was still far too early to sound caution over inflation, he added that any rise in prices should be watched closely in light of the current rock-bottom level of interest rates.
"The present level of interest rates takes into account zero inflation as a prerequisite," he said.
The BOJ has kept the official discount rate at a historical low of 0.5 percent since September 1995.
In contrast to import prices, domestic prices have been tame and the BOJ has said this has been due to supply and demand conditions in the economy, which have improved only moderately.
Domestic prices for the same period of February fell 0.2 percent from February of the previous year.
"But there is no guarantee that there won't be inflation when supply and demand improves," another BOJ official said.
